summary: This experimental RFC describes encoding VPN service information in an experimental IPv6 Destination Option called the VPN Service Option. One purpose is to show that it can be deployed in a production network.

eli5.summary: A packet carries a tag saying which private network it belongs to. This is an experiment to see if that works in real networks.

questions: vpn service information in destination option
what is the ipv6 vpn service option
how does ipv6 destination option carry vpn information
subtitle: An experiment that carries VPN service information in an IPv6 Destination Option instead of a separate tunnel label.

tldr.problem: Most VPN technologies need a non-IPv6 header such as MPLS, or an IP address per VPN, to tell the egress router which forwarding entry should handle the customer data.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router wraps customer data in an IPv6 header plus a Destination Options header holding a 32-bit VPN Service Option. The egress router uses that value to find a FIB entry and forward the data to the customer device.
tldr.outcome: This is an experiment using an experimental code point, so processing is off by default and participants are asked to publish results within one year.

today: RFC 9837 is an Experimental RFC, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification, and it asks participants to publish results within one year.

sections.title: Why Another VPN Encoding
sections.content:
Existing VPN technologies such as L3VPN, EVPN and SRv6 share a pattern. An ingress Provider Edge (PE) router wraps customer data in a tunnel header that carries service information. The egress PE looks that information up in its FIB. If it finds a match it strips the tunnel header and forwards the data to a Customer Edge (CE) device. If not, it discards the packet.

This RFC proposes encoding the service information in an IPv6 Destination Option called the VPN Service Option. The stated benefits are that no configuration is needed on CE devices, no non-IPv6 header such as MPLS is needed, many VPNs can sit on one egress PE, and no IP address per VPN is needed. It also does not rely on any particular control plane.
sections.eli5: Different VPN systems use different kinds of labels on their parcels. This one puts the label in a spot IPv6 already has for extra notes.

sections.title: The VPN Service Option
sections.content:
The option follows the normal IPv6 Destination Option layout from RFC 8200: Option Type, Opt Data Len and Option Data. Option Type MUST be 0x5E, the single code point reserved for RFC 3692-style experiments. Opt Data Len MUST be 4. Option Data is 32 bits of VPN service information that identifies a FIB entry on the egress PE.

A single VPN Service Option MAY appear in a Destination Options header that immediately precedes an upper-layer header, and MUST NOT appear in any other extension header. In the type byte, the two highest-order bits are 01, so a destination that does not recognize the option discards the packet. The third bit is 0, so the data cannot change along the path.
sections.eli5: The note is a small box with a type, a length and a 32-bit number. The number says which room the parcel goes to.

sections.title: Forwarding and Control Plane
sections.content:
The tunnel header built by the ingress PE MUST contain an IPv6 header and a Destination Options header that immediately precedes the customer data. The Destination Options header's Next Header MUST identify the customer data's protocol, and its Options field MUST contain exactly one VPN Service Option. Source and destination addresses represent interfaces on the ingress and egress PE, and SHOULD be chosen following RFC 6724.

The FIB can be populated by an operator using a CLI, by a controller using PCEP or NETCONF, or by a routing protocol. Routing protocol extensions for this option are outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: The sending router wraps the parcel and adds the sticker. How the receiving router learns what each sticker means can be set by a person, a controller, or a routing system.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
A VPN's security policy is that nodes outside it cannot inject traffic into it, and nodes inside it cannot send traffic outside it. Because PE routers cooperate to enforce this, no outside device may be able to impersonate an inside one.

On the global Internet, the tunnel between ingress and egress PE MUST be cryptographically protected by the IPv6 Authentication Header (RFC 4302) or ESP (RFC 4303). Inside a limited domain, edge nodes MUST keep access control lists that discard packets that contain a VPN Service Option and have a destination address inside the domain. The RFC notes that these mitigations are fail-open and need explicit configuration.
sections.eli5: Only trusted routers may stick or read these labels. Outsiders must be kept from forging them, either by locking the tunnel or by guarding the doors of the network.

sections.title: Deployment Risks and Experiment Goals
sections.content:
Only the ingress and egress PE process the option. Some networks discard packets with IPv6 Destination Options, which is an obstacle. The experimental code point could also collide with another experiment that uses the same value. Because of this, processing MUST be disabled by default and needs explicit configuration.

Participants should publish results within one year. They should cover the effort to deploy and to secure, how the FIB was populated, scale, interoperability, and whether OAM tools such as PING, TRACEROUTE, Wireshark and TCPDUMP worked.
sections.eli5: It is a trial run. Some networks throw away packets with extra notes, so the option stays switched off until someone turns it on, and testers report back how it went.

fields.name: Option Type
fields.desc: Selector for the VPN Service Option.

fields.name: Opt Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the option excluding the first two fields.

fields.name: Option Data
fields.desc: VPN service information identifying a FIB entry on the egress PE.
